fixes.explanation: Nobody doubled anything, baker. Baasha stopped. The text says that when he learned of it, he "…stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work." Doubling down would have been the opposite of that.

Close, because it does have to do with a border. But the text never mentions the Philistines here. Baasha went up against Judah and fortified Ramah "…to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah." So this was aimed at Asa's side, not at anybody else.

Ships coming in from Ophir? Not in this story, friend. The text says Asa took the silver and gold out of the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace. It was already in storage, so there was no dock to wait at and no one to wave at from the shore.

Shishak king of Egypt never shows up here, baker. The silver and gold went to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus. Egypt would've been a long walk in the wrong direction, and the messenger had Damascus on the mind.

Keeping the treaty is the opposite of what Asa asks, friend. He tells Ben-hadad, "Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me." The word he uses is break. Keep is the one thing he doesn't want.
Not finished, friend. The text says Baasha "…stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work." He stopped, and the work at Ramah was left behind. Finishing is the opposite of what happened.

This one is true, friend. The text says Asa brought all the men of Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. Then with these materials Asa built up Geba and Mizpah. So Baasha's leftovers went straight into Asa's building projects.

That's right, friend. Hanani tells Asa, "You have acted foolishly in this matter. From now on, therefore, you will be at war." Asa paid a pile of silver and gold to fix one problem. And Hanani says war is what's coming. That's one expensive deal.
The text doesn't say Asa sent Hanani out of Judah, friend. It says Asa became so enraged that he put the man in prison. That's what happened to the seer who brought him the message.
You got it, baker. Asa put Hanani in prison, and "…at the same time Asa oppressed some of the people." So Hanani wasn't the only one. This is a heavy part of the story.

That's what the text says, friend. In his illness Asa "…did not seek the LORD, but only the physicians." The problem wasn't the doctors. It was that the LORD wasn't the one he sought. I think that's a sad line to read.
